dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure certificates and Transport Layer Security (TLS) for an App Service
domanda: Fabrikam hosts a web app named app1 in an App Service plan that uses the Standard tier. The security team wants to secure several custom domains by using free App Service managed certificates instead of purchasing certificates. Which domain CANNOT be secured by a free App Service managed certificate?
opzione_a: www.fabrikam.com, mapped with a CNAME record that points directly to app1.azurewebsites.net
opzione_b: fabrikam.com, mapped with an A record that points to the app's inbound IP address
opzione_c: *.fabrikam.com, mapped with a CNAME record that points directly to app1.azurewebsites.net
opzione_d: shop.fabrikam.com, mapped with a CNAME record that points directly to app1.azurewebsites.net
spiegazione: Correct: *.fabrikam.com is a wildcard domain. The free App Service managed certificate explicitly does not support wildcard certificates, so this domain must be secured with an uploaded private certificate, an App Service certificate, or a certificate imported from Azure Key Vault. Why the others are wrong: www.fabrikam.com and shop.fabrikam.com are subdomains, which are supported as long as the CNAME record maps directly to <app-name>.azurewebsites.net (mapping to an intermediate CNAME value would block issuance and renewal, but that is not the case here). fabrikam.com is an apex/root domain, which is supported provided it has an A record pointing to the web app's IP address, the app has no IP restrictions that block internet reachability, and the root domain is not integrated with Azure Traffic Manager.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure certificates and Transport Layer Security (TLS) for an App Service
domanda: A web app named app1 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Standard tier. The custom domain www.contoso.com is mapped to app1 by using an A record at the domain registrar. To meet a compliance requirement for a dedicated certificate and a dedicated IP address, an administrator changes the existing binding for www.contoso.com from SNI SSL to IP-based SSL. Shortly afterward, users report that https://www.contoso.com returns an error, although https://app1.azurewebsites.net still works. What should you do to restore access?
opzione_a: Set the minimum inbound TLS version of app1 to 1.2 in the general settings of the app.
opzione_b: Update the A record at the domain registrar so that it points to the new dedicated inbound IP address that is shown on the app's Custom domains page.
opzione_c: Delete the IP-based SSL binding, recreate it as an SNI SSL binding, and add a TXT record named asuid for the domain.
opzione_d: Add a CNAME record for www that points to sni.app1.azurewebsites.net.
spiegazione: Correct: By default an app uses a shared public inbound IP address. When you bind a certificate by using IP-based SSL, App Service allocates a new, dedicated inbound IP address to the app. Any A record that pointed at the old shared address is now stale, so you must copy the new dedicated address from the app's Custom domains page and remap the A record to it. Why the others are wrong: Changing the minimum TLS version affects which TLS protocol versions clients may negotiate; it does not fix a name-resolution problem and 1.2 is already the default. Recreating the binding as SNI SSL would work around the issue but abandons the dedicated-IP compliance requirement, and the asuid TXT record is used for domain-ownership verification when adding the domain, not for restoring a binding. Adding a CNAME to sni.app1.azurewebsites.net is the remap step required when an SNI SSL binding exists on <app-name>.azurewebsites.net; it is not the remap for IP-based SSL, and a CNAME cannot be combined with the existing A-record mapping here.
tags: app service,ip based ssl,sni ssl,tls binding,dns,a record

sotto_argomento: Map an existing custom DNS name to an App Service
domanda: Northwind plans to map the root domain northwind.com to an App Service app named app2. The DNS zone for northwind.com is hosted at a third-party registrar. You must complete the mapping and let App Service verify ownership of the domain. Which set of DNS records should you create at the registrar?
opzione_a: An A record for the @ host that points to the app's IP address, and a TXT record named asuid that contains the domain verification ID
opzione_b: A CNAME record for the @ host that points to app2.azurewebsites.net, and a TXT record named asuid that contains the domain verification ID
opzione_c: An A record for the @ host that points to the app's IP address, and a CNAME record named asuid that points to app2.azurewebsites.net
opzione_d: A CNAME record for the @ host that points to app2.azurewebsites.net, and a TXT record named asuid.www that contains the domain verification ID
spiegazione: Correct: For a root (apex) domain, App Service documents an A record on the @ host that points to the app's IP address, plus a TXT record named asuid that holds the domain verification ID. App Service reads the asuid TXT record to confirm that you own the domain, which protects against subdomain takeover. Why the others are wrong: A CNAME record must not be used for a root domain; RFC 1912 forbids a CNAME coexisting with other records at the zone apex, and the documentation explicitly says not to use CNAME for the root domain. The verification record must be of type TXT, not CNAME, because App Service looks up the verification ID as text. The asuid.<subdomain> form (for example, asuid.www) is used for subdomains such as www.northwind.com; for the root domain the host is simply asuid.
tags: app service,custom domain,apex domain,a record,asuid,txt record

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure backup for an App Service
domanda: An app named app3 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier. Corporate policy requires that scheduled custom backups of app3 be written to a storage account named sa1. On sa1, public network access is denied and only selected virtual networks are allowed. You must configure the scheduled custom backups so that they succeed. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a private endpoint for app3 and set public network access for app3 to Disabled.
opzione_b: Enable virtual network integration for app3, grant the integration subnet access on sa1, and select the option to back up and restore over virtual network integration.
opzione_c: Assign a system-assigned managed identity to app3 and grant the identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on sa1.
opzione_d: Configure automatic backups for app3 and set sa1 as the backup destination.
spiegazione: Correct: Custom backups can target a firewall-protected storage account only when the app is integrated with a virtual network (or hosted in an App Service Environment v3), the storage account allows access from that virtual network, and the backup/restore over virtual network integration option is selected on the custom backup configuration. Why the others are wrong: A private endpoint on app3 controls inbound access to the app itself; it does nothing for the app's outbound call to the storage account. Managed identity authentication is not supported for App Service backup and restore, which requires a storage account that supports SAS-based authorization, so granting the identity an RBAC role does not enable the backup. Automatic backups require no configuration and are stored on the platform in the same datacenter as the App Service; you cannot point them at your own storage account, and they are not supported over a virtual network.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: An app named app4 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Standard tier and has a deployment slot named staging. A connection string named SqlDb is defined in both slots: the production slot points to a production database and the staging slot points to a test database. After the release team swaps staging into production, the production site begins writing to the test database. You must ensure that each slot keeps its own SqlDb value after future swaps, while application content continues to swap normally. What should you do?
opzione_a: Add the app setting WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_PRESERVE_DEFAULT_STICKY_SLOT_SETTINGS with a value of 0 to both slots.
opzione_b: In each slot, edit the SqlDb connection string and select Deployment slot setting.
opzione_c: Use swap with preview instead of a direct swap when promoting the staging slot.
opzione_d: Enable auto swap on the staging slot and set the target slot to production.
spiegazione: Correct: Connection strings are swapped by default. Marking the SqlDb connection string as a deployment slot setting (the slotSetting property, or --slot-settings in the Azure CLI) makes it slot specific, so each slot keeps its own value while the app content still swaps. Why the others are wrong: WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_PRESERVE_DEFAULT_STICKY_SLOT_SETTINGS=0 reverts the platform's default sticky behavior for protocol settings, IP restrictions, Always On, diagnostic log settings, and CORS; it applies to those marked settings only and would make them swappable, which is the opposite of the goal and does not affect connection strings. Swap with preview only pauses the swap so you can validate the source slot with the target slot's settings applied; it does not change which settings are swapped. Auto swap automates the promotion, but the connection string would still swap.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure networking settings for an App Service
domanda: Litware runs an internal line-of-business app named app5 in an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier. App5 must be reachable only from virtual machines in a hub-and-spoke topology and from the on-premises datacenter, which connects to the hub virtual network over ExpressRoute private peering. App5 must not be reachable from the public internet. Which networking feature should you configure?
opzione_a: Regional virtual network integration with outbound internet traffic routing enabled
opzione_b: An access restriction rule that is based on a service endpoint for the virtual machine subnet
opzione_c: A private endpoint for app5, and public network access set to Disabled
spiegazione: Correct: A private endpoint gives app5 a network interface with a private IP address from your virtual network, so clients in peered virtual networks and on-premises clients connected over ExpressRoute private peering can reach the app privately. Disabling public network access removes the default public entry point and completes the isolation. Why the others are wrong: Virtual network integration is an outbound-only feature. It lets the app call resources in the virtual network but explicitly does not grant inbound private access to the app, and routing all outbound traffic does not change that. A service endpoint based access restriction limits the public endpoint to selected Azure subnets, but the app keeps a public endpoint and on-premises clients arriving over ExpressRoute are not covered by a service endpoint rule. Hybrid Connections provide outbound access from the app to a TCP endpoint on-premises; they do not publish the app privately.
tags: app service,private endpoint,vnet integration,private site access,expressroute

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: An app named app6 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier and has a deployment slot named staging. Before a release, an engineer must document which configuration elements stay with the slot rather than follow the content when the two slots are swapped. No app setting or connection string has been marked as a deployment slot setting, and no swap-behavior override app settings are configured. Which configuration elements are NOT swapped? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
spiegazione: Correct: Custom domain names, managed identities, and virtual network integration are all documented as settings that are not swapped; they stay with the slot. The same list also includes publishing endpoints, non-public certificates and TLS/SSL settings, protocol settings such as HTTPS Only and TLS version, scale settings, WebJobs schedulers, IP restrictions, Always On, diagnostic log settings, CORS, and settings ending with _EXTENSION_VERSION. Why the others are wrong: App settings and connection strings are swapped by default and follow the content across a swap. They stay with the slot only when you explicitly select Deployment slot setting for them (the slotSetting property), which the scenario states has not been done.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure networking settings for an App Service
domanda: Contoso deploys a web app named app7 to an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier. App7 must connect to an Azure SQL database that is exposed only through a private endpoint in a virtual network named vnet1. In addition, app7 itself must be reachable only from clients inside vnet1 and must reject all traffic from the public internet. Which actions should you perform? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Enable regional virtual network integration for app7 by using a subnet in vnet1 that is delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms.
opzione_b: Create a private endpoint for app7 in vnet1 and set public network access for app7 to Disabled.
opzione_c: Link the privatelink.database.windows.net private DNS zone to vnet1 so that app7 resolves the database to its private endpoint address.
opzione_d: Create the private endpoint for app7 in the same subnet that is used for virtual network integration.
opzione_e: Add an access restriction rule to app7 that allows the AzureCloud service tag and set the unmatched rule action to Deny.
spiegazione: Correct: Virtual network integration on a delegated subnet gives app7 outbound access into vnet1, which is what lets it reach the database's private endpoint. A private endpoint for app7 plus public network access set to Disabled provides inbound private-only access and eliminates public exposure. Linking the privatelink.database.windows.net private DNS zone to vnet1 ensures the app's DNS lookup for the database resolves to the private IP address; without private DNS resolution the app would resolve the public name and the connection would fail. Why the others are wrong: The virtual network integration feature cannot use the same subnet as the private endpoint, so option D is unsupported. The AzureCloud service tag covers the public IP ranges of Azure services worldwide, which is far broader than vnet1 and would not restrict access to vnet1 clients; access restriction rules are also not evaluated for traffic arriving through a private endpoint.
tags: app service,private endpoint,vnet integration,private dns zone,subnet delegation

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Map an existing custom DNS name to an App Service
domanda: Adventure Works owns the public DNS zone adventureworks.com, which is hosted at a third-party registrar. You must map both adventureworks.com and www.adventureworks.com to an App Service app named app8, and secure each domain with a free App Service managed certificate. App8 currently runs in an App Service plan that uses the Free (F1) tier. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Record used to map adventureworks.com to app8: [A record | CNAME record | NS record]
opzione_b: Recommended record used to map www.adventureworks.com to app8: [A record | CNAME record | TXT record]
opzione_c: Record used to verify ownership of www.adventureworks.com: [TXT record named asuid.www | TXT record named asuid | CNAME record named asuid.www]
opzione_d: Minimum App Service plan tier required to create the managed certificates: [Free (F1) | Shared (D1) | Basic (B1)]
risposta_corretta: A record,CNAME record,TXT record named asuid.www,Basic (B1)
spiegazione: Correct: A root domain such as adventureworks.com must be mapped with an A record that points to the app's IP address; a CNAME record is not allowed at the zone apex. For a subdomain such as www.adventureworks.com the recommended record is a CNAME that points to the app's default hostname, because the app's inbound IP address can change while the default hostname does not. Domain ownership for a subdomain is verified with a TXT record named asuid.<subdomain>, so asuid.www here; the plain asuid host is used for a root or wildcard domain, and the record must be TXT, not CNAME. Free App Service managed certificates require the App Service plan to be in the Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated tier, so the plan must be scaled up from Free (F1); the Shared (D1) tier can host a custom domain but cannot create a managed certificate.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure backup for an App Service
domanda: A junior administrator is preparing a backup plan for several App Service apps and asks you to confirm the platform behavior of App Service backups. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Minimum App Service plan tier that supports backup and restore: [Free (F1) | Shared (D1) | Basic (B1)]
opzione_b: Maximum size of an automatic backup: [10 GB | 30 GB | 100 GB]
opzione_c: Maximum size of a custom backup: [4 GB | 10 GB | 30 GB]
opzione_d: Retention period of automatic backups: [7 days | 30 days | 90 days]
spiegazione: Correct: Backup and restore is supported in the Basic, Standard, Premium, and Isolated tiers; the Free and Shared tiers do not support it, and in the Basic tier you can back up and restore only the production slot. Automatic backups have a backup size of 30 GB, are created hourly, and are retained for 30 days; the retention schedule is not configurable. Custom backups have a maximum size of 10 GB, of which up to 4 GB can be a linked database, which is why 4 GB is a plausible but incorrect value for the total custom backup size. 100 GB and 7/90 days are not documented App Service backup values.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: An app named app9 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Standard tier and has a production slot and a staging slot. After the last swap, the operations team reports three findings: the Application Insights connection string that was configured only in staging is now live in production; the custom domain shop.contoso.com stayed on the production slot; and the virtual network integration configured on staging did not follow the content into production. No swap-behavior override app settings are configured. Select the correct option for each statement.
opzione_a: To keep APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING with each slot during a swap, you must: [Mark the setting as a deployment slot setting in both slots | Add the app setting WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_PRESERVE_DEFAULT_STICKY_SLOT_SETTINGS with a value of 0 to both slots | Store the value in Azure Key Vault and reference it from both slots]
opzione_b: Custom domain names during a swap are: [Swapped | Not swapped | Swapped only when HTTPS Only is disabled]
opzione_c: Virtual network integration during a swap is: [Swapped | Not swapped | Swapped only in the Premium v3 and Isolated v2 tiers]
opzione_d: To validate the staging slot with the production slot's settings applied before completing the swap, use: [Swap with preview | Auto swap | Traffic routing with the x-ms-routing-name query parameter]
risposta_corretta: Mark the setting as a deployment slot setting in both slots,Not swapped,Not swapped,Swap with preview
spiegazione: Correct: App settings are swapped by default, so an instrumentation or connection-string app setting follows the content into production unless it is marked as a deployment slot setting (slotSetting) in the slots. The override app setting WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_PRESERVE_DEFAULT_STICKY_SLOT_SETTINGS=0 only reverts the default sticky behavior of protocol settings, IP restrictions, Always On, diagnostic log settings, and CORS; it does not make an app setting slot specific. A Key Vault reference changes where the secret is stored, not whether the setting swaps. Custom domain names and virtual network integration are both on the documented list of settings that are not swapped, in every tier. Swap with preview performs the first phase of the swap, applying the target slot's slot-specific settings to the source slot and pausing so you can validate before completing; auto swap promotes automatically with no validation pause, and x-ms-routing-name traffic routing sends a share of live users to a slot rather than validating a pending swap.
tags: app service,deployment slots,swap with preview,sticky settings,custom domain,vnet integration

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure networking settings for an App Service
domanda: A web app named app10 runs in an App Service plan named plan1 that uses the Premium v3 tier. Regional virtual network integration is enabled for app10 by using a subnet named Subnet1 in a virtual network named vnet1. Evaluate each of the following statements about this configuration and indicate whether it is true. 1) Regional virtual network integration allows virtual machines in vnet1 to reach app10 by using a private IP address. 2) Subnet1 must be delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms and cannot be shared with resources of other types. 3) Plan1 can have virtual network integration with up to two subnets, but app10 can use only one virtual network integration at a time.
opzione_a: Regional virtual network integration allows virtual machines in vnet1 to reach app10 by using a private IP address.
opzione_b: Subnet1 must be delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms and cannot be shared with resources of other types.
opzione_c: Plan1 can have virtual network integration with up to two subnets, but app10 can use only one virtual network integration at a time.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: virtual network integration is used only to make outbound calls from the app into the virtual network. It gives the app access to resources in the virtual network but does not grant inbound private access to the app; for inbound private access you must use a private endpoint. Statement 2 is Yes: virtual network integration depends on a dedicated subnet that is delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms, and the integration subnet cannot be shared with other resource types (an orphaned Microsoft.Web/serverFarms delegation is precisely what blocks subnet reuse after an app is deleted without disconnecting). Statement 3 is Yes: the feature supports two virtual interfaces per worker, which means an App Service plan can integrate with up to two subnets/virtual networks, while any single app can have only one virtual network integration at a given time.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Map an existing custom DNS name to an App Service
domanda: Wide World Importers hosts a web app named app11 in an App Service plan that uses the Free (F1) tier. You must map the existing custom domain www.wideworldimporters.com to app11, verify ownership of the domain, and secure the domain with a free App Service managed certificate. The DNS zone is managed at a third-party registrar. Drag the actions into the correct order to complete the task with the fewest steps.
opzione_a: In the app's Custom domains page, select Add custom domain, enter www.wideworldimporters.com, and copy the domain verification ID and the required record values.
opzione_b: Scale the App Service plan up from the Free (F1) tier to the Basic (B1) tier.
opzione_c: In the Add custom domain dialog, select Validate, confirm that both records show a green check mark, and then select Add.
opzione_d: At the registrar, create a CNAME record for the www host that points to app11.azurewebsites.net, and a TXT record named asuid.www that contains the domain verification ID.
opzione_e: Create an App Service managed certificate for www.wideworldimporters.com and add the TLS/SSL binding by using SNI SSL.
spiegazione: Correct order: (1) Scale up from Free (F1). Mapping a custom domain requires a paid tier, and a free App Service managed certificate additionally requires Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated, so Basic (B1) satisfies both and must come first. (2) Open Add custom domain and enter the fully qualified domain name to obtain the domain verification ID and the record values you need. (3) Create the DNS records at the registrar: for a subdomain, a CNAME for www pointing directly to app11.azurewebsites.net (mapping to an intermediate CNAME value would block managed certificate issuance and renewal) plus a TXT record named asuid.www holding the verification ID. (4) Return to the portal and select Validate, then Add; validation reads the records you just created, so it cannot precede them. (5) Only after the domain is mapped and validated can you create the managed certificate for it and bind it. SNI SSL is the correct binding type here because it needs no dedicated IP address and no further DNS remapping.
tags: app service,custom domain,cname,asuid,managed certificate,sni ssl,scale up
